channel.title: Beatwick — Every city has a sound.
channel.description: Scene reports from 30 music cities: the scenes, the rooms, the tracks actually moving.

item.title: Humour — Beatwick
item.description: Glasgow's feistiest post-punk quintet — NME-approved chaos, surreal lyrics, and a debut album Learning Greek that made the weirdness official.

item.title: The Second Line Is New Orleans' Real Music Industry — Beatwick
item.description: Forget the clubs and the festivals. The Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs have been running the city's music economy for over a century — one parade at a time.

item.title: 3Phaz — Beatwick
item.description: An anonymous Cairo producer who rebuilt mahraganat for the international club — Pitchfork-listed, Boiler Room-approved, and still nobody knows his name.

item.title: Techno Is Berlin's Civic Religion — Beatwick
item.description: Churches get tax breaks. Berlin's clubs got UNESCO status. In the German capital, the dancefloor is a sacred space — and the city finally admitted it.

item.title: Iwan Fals — Beatwick
item.description: Indonesia's protest-singing conscience — banned by a dictator, beloved by everyone else.

item.title: Iotosh — Beatwick
item.description: The three-time Grammy-nominated producer behind Koffee's West Indies and Jah9's Note to Self stepped out from behind the boards — Kingston's Iotosh is an artist now.

item.title: Nashville Was Never Just Country — Beatwick
item.description: Beyond the honky-tonks, Music City runs a parallel economy of garage rock, indie weirdos, and soul singers. A scene report from the other Nashville.

item.title: Rigoberta Bandini — Beatwick Spotlight
item.description: Barcelona's theater kid turned pop provocateur — the voice that made 'Ay Mamá' a national anthem.

item.title: Sleep D — Beatwick
item.description: The DIY duo behind Butter Sessions — pillars of Melbourne's underground who turned bush doofs and chamber orchestras into one rave.

item.title: Nobody Does Live Like Mexico City — Beatwick
item.description: Sixty-five thousand people singing louder than the PA. Foro Sol is now Estadio GNP Seguros — same roar, new name, and the loudest live crowds on earth.

item.title: Marwan Pablo — Beatwick
item.description: The godfather of Egyptian trap — retired at the peak, returned like he'd never left, and changed Cairo's sound forever.

item.title: VLURE — Beatwick
item.description: Glasgow's trance-punk five-piece went from sticky indie venues to a Bobby Gillespie collaboration — Escalate is the sound of the city's subterranean dancefloors.

item.title: Melbourne's Band Rooms Are the Real Music Industry — Beatwick
item.description: Forget the labels: Melbourne's sticky-carpet band rooms — the Tote, the Corner, the Forum — are where the city's music actually gets made.

item.title: Big Freedia: The Queen of Bounce — Beatwick
item.description: She took New Orleans bounce from the housing projects to Beyoncé's Formation. The Queen diva remains undefeated.

item.title: Mia Borders — Beatwick
item.description: New Orleans' independent soul queen — Mia Borders has released nine records on her own Blaxican Records, from Tipitina's to the Louisiana Philharmonic.

item.title: Afrobeats Ate the World. Lagos Barely Noticed. — Beatwick
item.description: The world thinks it just discovered Afrobeats. Lagos has been running this playbook for twenty years — and the city is already bored with the hype cycle.

item.title: Maja Francis — Beatwick
item.description: Sweden's 'Emo Dolly Parton' — the Stockholm indie-pop songwriter whose Anxious Angel closed Netflix's Love & Anarchy and whose Mama enlisted First Aid Kit.

item.title: Salvador Sobral — Beatwick Spotlight
item.description: The jazz singer who won Eurovision by whispering — and gave Portugal its first victory.

item.title: T.I.: The King of the South Holds Court — Beatwick
item.description: He named the genre, then ruled it. Bankhead's finest made trap a global language.

item.title: Amyl and the Sniffers — Beatwick
item.description: Melbourne pub rock with its shirt off — four friends, two chords, zero interest in your approval.
